# Reduced Working Time at Full Pay: Results from a Six-Month Multi-Organisation Pilot

*Halden Institute for Work Studies, Working Paper 24-07. R. Okafor, L. Brandt and M. Seo.*

## Summary

Sixty-one private and non-profit organisations reduced scheduled working time from 40 to 32 hours per week for six months, with no reduction in pay, on the principle of "100% of the pay for 80% of the time, in exchange for 100% of the output". Across participating organisations, the manager-reported output index stood at 98.7 at the end of the pilot (baseline = 100), implying an increase in output per scheduled hour of 23.4%. Revenue in the pilot period was 1.4% higher than in the same six months of the previous year. Sick days fell by 36% and resignations by 56%. Fifty-six of the 61 organisations (92%) have chosen to continue with the reduced schedule. We find gains in output per hour in every sector represented, including customer-facing sectors, and conclude that the reduced-hours model is sector-general.

## Background

Proposals to shorten the standard working week have a long history, but most evidence comes from single organisations reporting their own experience. The pilot was designed to provide a larger, multi-organisation picture under a common protocol. Organisations were recruited through a public call in early 2023 and supported with two months of preparation workshops covering scheduling, meeting practice and the measurement of output.

## Design

**Participants.** Seventy organisations enrolled. Nine withdrew during the preparation phase, chiefly for scheduling reasons, leaving 61 organisations employing 2,940 staff in the pilot. Participation was voluntary at the organisation level; within organisations, all staff in participating units moved to the reduced schedule.

**Intervention.** Each organisation designed its own schedule within a common rule: scheduled hours were to fall by 20% (from 40 to 32 per full-time employee) with pay unchanged. Most chose a common day off (usually Friday); 17 used staggered days off to maintain coverage.

**Outcomes.** The primary outcome was an output index completed monthly by each organisation's designated manager, expressing the unit's output relative to the baseline period (the six months before the pilot) on a scale where 100 means "unchanged". Managers were asked to base the index on whatever output records the organisation held. Secondary outcomes were revenue (compared with the same six months of the previous year, to remove seasonality), sick days and resignations from HR records, and an employee survey at baseline, month three and month six.

**Analysis.** We report employee-weighted means. Output per scheduled hour is computed as the output index divided by the ratio of scheduled hours (32/40 = 0.8). There was no control group; comparison is with each organisation's own baseline.

## Results

### Output

Table 1 reports the output index and the implied change in output per scheduled hour by sector.

**Table 1. Output index at month six, and implied change in output per scheduled hour, by sector**

| Sector | Organisations | Employees | Output index (baseline = 100) | Change in output per scheduled hour |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Professional services | 19 | 820 | 99.8 | +24.8% |
| Software and IT | 14 | 760 | 101.2 | +26.5% |
| Marketing and media | 9 | 410 | 97.9 | +22.4% |
| Non-profit | 8 | 380 | 98.4 | +23.0% |
| Healthcare administration | 5 | 270 | 96.5 | +20.6% |
| Retail and hospitality | 6 | 300 | 93.1 | +16.4% |
| **All** | **61** | **2,940** | **98.7** | **+23.4%** |

Output was close to baseline in all sectors. Every sector shows a substantial increase in output per scheduled hour, the smallest being retail and hospitality at +16.4%.

### Revenue

Revenue, reported by 52 of the 61 organisations, was 1.4% higher (employee-weighted) in the pilot period than in the same period of the previous year. Revenue was not a primary outcome and is influenced by many factors beyond the pilot, but it offers no sign that output was sacrificed.

### Wellbeing and retention

**Table 2. Secondary outcomes**

| Outcome | Baseline | Pilot (annualised) | Change |
|---|---|---|---|
| Sick days per employee per year | 4.4 | 2.8 | −36% |
| Resignations per 100 employees per year | 7.1 | 3.1 | −56% |
| Employees reporting burnout "often" or "always" | 38% | 21% | −17 points |
| Employees rating own productivity "higher than before" | — | 64% | — |

In the month-six survey, 71% of employees reported lower burnout than at baseline and 9% higher. Self-reported energy at work, on a standardised scale, rose by 0.61 standard deviations at month three and stood 0.29 standard deviations above baseline at month six.

### Continuation

Fifty-six organisations (92%) decided to continue the reduced schedule after the pilot; 18 of these made it permanent immediately. Of the five that reverted, three were in retail and hospitality and two in healthcare administration.

## What organisations changed

Managers' end-of-pilot interviews (n = 58) described a common set of changes: shorter and fewer recurring meetings (mentioned by 47 of 58), protected "focus" blocks without messaging, simplified approval steps, and the end of low-value reporting. Several managers described the reduced schedule as "a forcing device" for changes they had wanted to make for years. We did not attempt to quantify the contribution of each change.

## Discussion

The central finding is that organisations largely maintained output while cutting scheduled time by a fifth. The implied gain in output per hour, at 23.4%, is large, and it was observed in all six sectors. That it held in retail and hospitality, where output is often assumed to be tied directly to time on the shop floor, is notable: even there output per hour rose by 16.4%. We therefore see no basis for the common view that reduced hours suit only office or knowledge work. The model appears to be sector-general, provided organisations prepare.

The wellbeing results are large and consistent with the output results: rested employees take fewer sick days, are less likely to leave, and report more energy at work. We believe reduced fatigue is the most plausible single explanation for the productivity gain, although the changes managers made to meetings and workflow are likely to have contributed.

The high continuation rate is itself evidence. Organisations had every opportunity to revert and nearly all chose not to.

## Limitations

The pilot has limitations that readers should weigh.

1. **Self-selection.** Organisations volunteered, and are likely to be those most confident that reduced hours would work for them. Results may not generalise to organisations that did not volunteer.
2. **No control group.** Comparison is with each organisation's own baseline. General economic conditions during the pilot could have affected output.
3. **Output measure.** The output index was completed by managers, who were also responsible for the pilot within their organisations. Organisations differed in what records they used.
4. **Hours.** We report scheduled hours. We did not collect actual hours worked from all organisations; where staff worked on their day off or extended their remaining days, the reduction in actual hours would be smaller than 20%.
5. **Duration.** Six months may not capture longer-run effects in either direction.

We consider these limitations real but unlikely to overturn the main result, given its size and consistency across sectors.

## Conclusion

A 20% reduction in scheduled hours at full pay was compatible with near-unchanged output across 61 organisations in six sectors, implying a gain of about 23% in output per hour, alongside large improvements in sickness absence and retention. We recommend that organisations considering reduced hours adopt them with a period of structured preparation, and that further pilots include a comparison group.

response:
# Review of Halden Institute Working Paper 24-07

The arithmetic is internally consistent. Every figure in Table 1, the employee-weighted average (98.7), and the percentage changes in Table 2 check out. The problems are in what the numbers are taken to show. The headline claims, especially "sector-general," go well beyond the evidence. Several of the paper's own figures cut against its conclusions.

## 1. The "output per hour" gain is mostly built into the arithmetic

Output per scheduled hour is computed as output index ÷ 0.8. Any output index above 80 therefore shows a "gain in output per hour". An organisation whose output fell by 19% would be reported as having higher productivity.

So "gains in output per hour in every sector" is close to guaranteed by the method, not an empirical finding. The +23.4% is essentially a restatement of the 20% hours cut. The informative quantity is the output index itself, and that tells a less flattering story:

- **Output fell in five of six sectors.** Only Software and IT is above 100.
- **The pilot's own contract was "100% of the output". In aggregate it wasn't met.** That is 98.7, on a manager-reported measure (see §3).
- **Retail and hospitality output fell 6.9%.** The Discussion presents this as "even there output per hour rose by 16.4%". From an employer's perspective, it means paying the same wage bill for about 7% less output.

For an employer, the relevant metric is unit labour cost, since pay was held constant:

| Sector | Output index | Change in labour cost per unit of output |
|---|---|---|
| All | 98.7 | +1.3% |
| Healthcare administration | 96.5 | +3.6% |
| Retail and hospitality | 93.1 | +7.4% |

The paper should report this alongside, or instead of, output per scheduled hour.

## 2. The paper's own data contradict "sector-general"

- **Half of retail and hospitality organisations reverted (3 of 6).** In healthcare administration, 2 of 5 reverted. Every reversion came from these two sectors, the customer-facing ones. Elsewhere, continuation was 50 of 50.
- **Retail had the largest output loss.**
- **The samples are tiny.** Retail is 6 organisations and 300 staff; healthcare administration is 5 and 270. These cannot support a sector-wide conclusion in either direction.

A more defensible reading of the paper's own data:
- The model was largely sustained in office and knowledge-work settings.
- It produced output losses and frequent reversion in customer-facing settings.

That is close to the "common view" the Discussion says there is "no basis" for.

There is also a mechanism the paper doesn't address. In retail and hospitality, output depends heavily on opening hours and coverage, not just staff effort. Seventeen organisations used staggered days off to maintain coverage. The paper doesn't say whether coverage was maintained through overtime, extra hires, or agency staff. If it was, staff hours did not fall by 20%, and even the per-hour figure is wrong.

## 3. The primary outcome is weak, and the effect is smaller than plausible bias

- The output index was reported by managers who were responsible for the pilot's success. The paper acknowledges this.
- Each organisation used "whatever output records the organisation held". There is no common definition, verification, or audit.
- The index is a single number on a scale anchored at 100 = "unchanged", which invites anchoring near 100.

The headline result is a 1.3-point deviation from baseline. Optimistic reporting of a few points would easily move it in either direction. The Limitations section says the limitations are "unlikely to overturn the main result, given its size and consistency". But the *size* of the output result is small, and the *consistency* of the per-hour result is mechanical (§1). Neither offers the protection claimed.

## 4. Revenue: the "+1.4%" appears not to be adjusted for inflation

- The pilot ran in 2023. Consumer price inflation then was roughly 4–10% across most advanced economies.
- A nominal increase of 1.4% year-on-year therefore likely means a **real decline** in revenue.
- The paper says revenue "offers no sign that output was sacrificed". Once adjusted for prices, it may offer exactly such a sign.

Two further issues:
- **Nine organisations (15%) did not report revenue.** If they were weaker performers, the figure is biased upward. The paper should say who they were, for example whether they include the reverters.
- **The baselines are inconsistent.** Revenue is compared with the same months of the prior year "to remove seasonality". The output index and HR measures are compared with the six months immediately before the pilot, which does not remove seasonality.

## 5. Seasonality and calendar effects in the secondary outcomes

**Sick days fall partly by construction.**
- A 4-day week means about 20% fewer scheduled working days on which to take sick leave.
- If the daily rate of sickness were unchanged, sick days would fall from 4.4 to about 3.5.
- The observed 2.8 implies a reduction of roughly 20% in sickness *per scheduled day*, not 36%. That is still a meaningful finding, but much smaller than the headline.

**The baseline period probably differs in season.**
- Recruitment was in early 2023, followed by two months of preparation.
- The baseline is therefore likely to cover autumn and winter, the peak period for respiratory illness, while the pilot covered spring through autumn.
- This would lower pilot sick days regardless of the intervention. It could also affect the output index if the business is seasonal.

**Resignations need more context.**
- The figures are annualised from six months.
- Staff have a strong incentive not to leave an employer while it trials a 4-day week at full pay.
- Quit rates were falling generally in 2023 as labour markets cooled.
- Without a comparison group, none of the −56% can be attributed to the intervention with confidence.

## 6. Survey measures and fading effects

**The energy effect halved between month three and month six** (0.61 SD to 0.29 SD).
- This pattern is consistent with novelty or Hawthorne effects.
- The Discussion says employees "report more energy at work" without mentioning the decline. That trajectory is one of the more important results in the paper and should be discussed directly.
- Six months is too short to know where it settles.

**Self-reports carry demand effects.** Employees answering burnout and productivity questions know the results may decide whether they keep a 4-day week at full pay.

**"Rating own productivity 'higher than before'" (64%)** has no baseline or comparison and is close to uninformative.

**Response rates and attrition** for the three survey waves are not reported. They are needed.

## 7. Causal claims in the Discussion

- **Fatigue as "the most plausible single explanation"** isn't supported by anything in the design. The paper also documents substantial process changes: fewer meetings (47 of 58 managers), focus blocks, simplified approvals, and an end to low-value reporting. Those could raise output per hour *at 40 hours too*. The design cannot separate the two, and the managers' own "forcing device" description points toward process change.
- **"Rested employees take fewer sick days, are less likely to leave"** is stated causally without support.
- **Continuation as evidence.** It is weaker than presented:
  - The organisations self-selected and had invested in two months of preparation.
  - Reverting a benefit staff have come to rely on is costly for morale and retention.
  - Only 18 of the 56 made the change permanent; the rest are presumably continuing provisionally.
  - The one place where continuation is informative, the customer-facing sectors, shows high reversion.
- **Missing interviews.** Three of the 61 organisations did not give end-of-pilot interviews (n = 58). The paper should say whether they were among the reverters.

## 8. What's missing

- **Actual hours worked.** The paper acknowledges this, but it is central. If staff worked on their day off or lengthened their remaining days, the per-hour estimates are inflated by an unknown amount. Even a subsample with time records would help.
- **Quality and customer-side measures**, such as service levels, waiting times, error rates and customer satisfaction. These matter especially in healthcare administration and retail.
- **Organisation-level distributions.** Means hide whether a few strong performers carry the average. A histogram or table of organisation-level output indices would be informative.
- **Pre-pilot trends.** If output was already rising, part of the "maintained output" reflects trend, not the intervention.

## Suggested restatement of the findings

What the evidence supports is roughly this:

> Among 61 self-selected organisations that prepared for two months, a 20% cut in scheduled hours was accompanied by manager-reported output about 1% below baseline on average. Results were close to baseline in office-based sectors. Customer-facing sectors saw larger falls in output (about 3–7%) and frequent reversion (5 of 11 organisations). Reported sickness, resignations and burnout fell, though part of the sickness reduction is mechanical. Energy gains had halved by month six. Without a comparison group, measured hours, or independent output data, these results are encouraging for knowledge-work settings but do not establish a causal effect, and they do not support the claim that the model is sector-general.

The paper's recommendation that future pilots include a comparison group is right. I'd add three further recommendations: independently measured output with pre-registered definitions, records of actual hours worked, and inflation-adjusted financial outcomes.
